title: Ecclesiastes

stories.title: 🌬️ Ecclesiastes 1
summaryBullets: These are the words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem: (1:1).
“Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!” (1:2).
What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun? (1:3).
Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever. (1:4).
The sun rises and the sun sets; it hurries back to where it rises. (1:5).
The wind blows southward, then turns northward; round and round it swirls, ever returning on its course. (1:6).
All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full; to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow. (1:7).
All things are wearisome, more than one can describe; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing. (1:8).
What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun. (1:9).
Is there a case where one can say, “Look, this is new”? It has already existed in the ages before us. (1:10).
There is no remembrance of those who came before, and those yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow after. (1:11).
I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem. (1:12).
And I set my mind to seek and explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven. What a miserable task God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them! (1:13).
I have seen all the things that are done under the sun, and have found them all to be futile, a pursuit of the wind. (1:14).
What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted. (1:15).
I said to myself, “Behold, I have grown and increased in wisdom beyond all those before me who were over Jerusalem, and my mind has observed a wealth of wisdom and knowledge.” (1:16).
So I set my mind to know wisdom and madness and folly; I learned that this, too, is a pursuit of the wind. (1:17).
For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases. (1:18).
crossRefs: Ecclesiastes 12:8: Refrain repeated: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.”
Psalm 90:9-10: Human days pass quickly and end with a sigh.
Job 7:6-7: Days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle; life a breath.
Jeremiah 2:13: Water imagery: broken cisterns that hold no water (contrast with flowing streams).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֹהֶלֶת (Qohelet), Greek (LXX): Ἐκκλησιαστής (Ekklēsiastēs), Aramaic: קהלת
translationNotes.note: Title meaning “assembler/convener.” Not rendered as a personal name in the text beyond the title line.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֶבֶל (hevel, ‘breath/vapor’), Greek (LXX): ματαιότης (mataiotēs), Aramaic: הֲבֵל (havel)
translationNotes.note: A repeated term in the book. Translations vary: vanity, vapor, breath.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִתְרוֹן (yitron), Greek (LXX): περισσεία / ὠφέλεια, Aramaic: ייתרון
translationNotes.note: Advantage/surplus. Asked in 1:3 regarding toil.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ (taḥat ha-shamesh), Greek (LXX): ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιον, Aramaic: תחת שמשא
translationNotes.note: Repeated locale phrase for activities described in the book.

stories.keyTakeaway: Qohelet states the motto about vanity, observes repeating cycles, questions profit in toil under the sun, and notes fading remembrance.

stories.title: 🧪 Ecclesiastes 2
summaryBullets: I said to myself, “Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!” But it proved to be futile. (2:1).
I said of laughter, “It is folly,” and of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?” (2:2).

I sought to cheer my body with wine and to embrace folly— my mind still guiding me with wisdom— until I could see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives. (2:3).
I expanded my pursuits. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. (2:4).
I made gardens and parks for myself, where I planted all kinds of fruit trees. (2:5).
I built reservoirs to water my groves of flourishing trees. (2:6).
I acquired menservants and maidservants, and servants were born in my house. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before me, (2:7).
and I accumulated for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I gathered to myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men — many concubines. (2:8).
So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me. (2:9).
Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure. For my heart took delight in all my work, and this was the reward for all my labor. (2:10).

Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun. (2:11).
Then I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly; for what more can the king’s successor do than what has already been accomplished? (2:12).
And I saw that wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness: (2:13).
The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both. (2:14).
So I said to myself, “The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?” And I said to myself that this too is futile. (2:15).
For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come. Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool! (2:16).
So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind. (2:17).
I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me. (2:18).
And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish? Yet he will take over all the labor at which I have worked skillfully under the sun. This too is futile. (2:19).
So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun. (2:20).
When there is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, this too is futile and a great evil. (2:21).
For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun? (2:22).
Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile. (2:23).
Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God. (2:24).
For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment? (2:25).

To the man who is pleasing in His sight, He gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind. (2:26).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 7:1-12: Royal house-building projects in Jerusalem.
1 Kings 10:14-23: Wealth, silver, gold, and goods gathered in Jerusalem.
Ecclesiastes 6:2: Wealth not enjoyed by its owner noted elsewhere in the book.
Psalm 127:1-2: Labor and sleeplessness without gift of rest.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רְעוּת רוּחַ (reʿut ruach), Greek (LXX): προαίρεσις/νεφέλης (var.), Aramaic: רעות רוחא
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic phrase for a futile chase (1:14) (2:11) (2:17) (2:26).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁדָּה וְשִׁדּוֹת (shiddah ve-shiddot), Greek (LXX): ᾠδούς (singers) in some traditions, Aramaic: שדתא ושדותא
translationNotes.note: Rare terms in (2:8) translations vary (e.g., “concubines,” “many delights”). Retained here as the Hebrew expression.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱכֹל וּשְׁתֵה (ekhol u-shteh), Greek (LXX): φάγειν καὶ πεῖν, Aramaic: אכול ושתי
translationNotes.note: Formula recurring in Ecclesiastes for simple enjoyment associated with toil (2:24-25).

stories.keyTakeaway: Qohelet reports royal-scale tests of wisdom, pleasure, and work, finds them vapor-like before the common fate, and states that enjoyment of toil is given from the hand of God.

stories.title: ⏳ Ecclesiastes 3
summaryBullets: To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven: (3:1).
a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot, (3:2).
a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build, (3:3).
a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, (3:4).
a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing, (3:5).
a time to search and a time to count as lost, a time to keep and a time to discard, (3:6).
a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, (3:7).
a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace. (3:8).
What does the worker gain from his toil? (3:9).
I have seen the burden that God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them. (3:10).
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end. (3:11).
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live, (3:12).
and also that every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor — this is the gift of God. (3:13).
I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him. (3:14).
What exists has already been, and what will be has already been, for God will call to account what has passed. (3:15).
Furthermore, I saw under the sun that in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness. (3:16).
I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” (3:17).
I said to myself, “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” (3:18).
For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other — they all have the same breath. Man has no advantage over the animals, since everything is futile. (3:19).
All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust. (3:20).
Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth? (3:21).
I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will come after him? (3:22).
crossRefs: Psalm 31:15: “My times are in your hand.”
Job 14:5: Human days and bounds determined.
Ecclesiastes 8:6-7: There is a time and judgment for every matter, yet people do not know what will be.
Acts 17:26: Times and boundaries appointed (stated in a later context).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵת / זְמָן (ʿet / zeman), Greek (LXX): καιρός, Aramaic: זמן
translationNotes.note: Terms for an appointed occasion (3:1-8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לַהֲרֹג (laharog), Qal infinitive of הָרַג (harag), Greek (LXX): ἀποκτεῖναι, Aramaic: למקטל
translationNotes.note: General verb meaning ‘to kill/slay,’ used for varied kinds of killing (e.g., warfare, judicial execution, and even unlawful killing in some contexts). It is broader than רָצַח (ratsach, ‘murder’), the verb in the Sixth Commandment (Exod 20:13) (Deut 5:17). The poem lists contrasted times (‘a time to kill… a time to heal’) as observations about human experience and timing; the line itself does not specify moral status.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יָפֶה בְּעִתּוֹ (yafeh beʿitto), Greek (LXX): καλὸν ἐν καιρῷ, Aramaic: שפיר בזמניה
translationNotes.note: Statement about fit/appropriate timing (3:11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָעֹלָם (ha-ʿolam), Greek (LXX): τὸν αἰῶνα, Aramaic: עלמא
translationNotes.note: Term rendered “eternity/age.” The verse says humans cannot find out God’s work from beginning to end (3:11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִירְאוּ מִלְּפָנָיו (yirʾu milfanav), Greek (LXX): φοβῶνται ἀπὸ προσώπου αὐτοῦ, Aramaic: ידחלון מן קדםוי
translationNotes.note: Result stated in 3:14 regarding God’s enduring work.

stories.keyTakeaway: Qohelet lists appointed times, states that God’s enduring work and gift of enjoyment stand alongside human inability to discover His total work.

headings.text: To Everything There Is a Season

stories.title: ⚖️ Ecclesiastes 4
summaryBullets: Again I looked, and I considered all the oppression taking place under the sun. I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter. (4:1).
So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive. (4:2).
But better than both is he who has not yet existed, who has not seen the evil that is done under the sun. (4:3).
I saw that all labor and success spring from a man’s envy of his neighbor. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind. (4:4).
The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh. (4:5).
Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind. (4:6).
Again, I saw futility under the sun. (4:7).

There is a man all alone, without even a son or brother. And though there is no end to his labor, his eyes are still not content with his wealth: “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” This too is futile — a miserable task. (4:8).
Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor. (4:9).
For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up! (4:10).
Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone? (4:11).
And though one may be overpowered, two can resist. Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. (4:12).
Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning. (4:13).
For the youth has come from the prison to the kingship, though he was born poor in his own kingdom. (4:14).
I saw that all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king. (4:15).
There is no limit to all the people who were before them. Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind. (4:16).
crossRefs: Genesis 3:19: “Dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”
Psalm 82:1-4: Judgment in the assembly; defend the weak and needy.
Proverbs 14:30: Envy rots the bones (cf. 4:4).
Job 30:28-31: Lament over oppression and grief under the sun.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹשֶׁק / עֹשֵׁק (ʿosheq / ʿosheq), Greek (LXX): συκοφαντία/καταδυναστεία, Aramaic: עשוקא
translationNotes.note: Used for exploitation or abuse of power (4:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִנְאָה (qinʾāh), Greek: ζῆλος, Aramaic: קנאה
translationNotes.note: Named as a driver of toil and skill in 4:4.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חוּט הַמְשֻׁלָּשׁ (ḥut ha-meshullash); Greek: τὸ τριπλοῦν σχοινίον
translationNotes.note: Image for strength in companionship (4:12).

stories.keyTakeaway: Qohelet observes injustice and oppression, the common fate of death, envy-driven toil, the advantage of companionship, and the short memory of crowds for rulers.

stories.title: 🕍 Ecclesiastes 5
summaryBullets: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, who do not know that they do wrong. (5:1).
Do not be quick to speak, and do not be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few. (5:2).
As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool comes with many words. (5:3).
When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow. (5:4).
It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it. (5:5).
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake. Why should God be angry with your words and destroy the work of your hands? (5:6).
For as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Therefore, fear God. (5:7).

If you see the oppression of the poor and the denial of justice and righteousness in the province, do not be astonished at the matter; for one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them. (5:8).
The produce of the earth is taken by all; the king himself profits from the fields. (5:9).
He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. This too is futile. (5:10).
When good things increase, so do those who consume them; what then is the profit to the owner, except to behold them with his eyes? (5:11).
The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep. (5:12).
There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner, (5:13).
or wealth lost in a failed venture, so when that man has a son there is nothing to pass on. (5:14).
As a man came from his mother’s womb, so he will depart again, naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands. (5:15).
This too is a grievous affliction: Exactly as a man is born, so he will depart. What does he gain as he toils for the wind? (5:16).
Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger. (5:17).

Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him — for this is his lot. (5:18).
Furthermore, God has given riches and wealth to every man, and He has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor. This is a gift from God. (5:19).
For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart. (5:20).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 23:21-23: Vows to the LORD must be performed.
Numbers 30:2: A man shall not break his word; he shall do according to what he has vowed.
Proverbs 10:19: In many words transgression is not lacking.
Matthew 5:33-37: On oaths and truthful speech.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶבַח כְּסִילִים (zevaḥ kesilim), Greek (LXX): θυσία ἀφρόνων, Aramaic: דבח דכסילא
translationNotes.note: An offering presented without understanding/obedience (5:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶדֶר (neder), Greek: εὐχή, Aramaic: נידרא (nidra)
translationNotes.note: A pledged promise to God that binds the speaker (5:4-5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַלְאָךְ (malʾakh, ‘messenger’), Greek: ἄγγελος, Aramaic: מלאכא
translationNotes.note: Named official/messenger before whom excuses are not to be made (5:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְרָא אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים (yera et-ha’Elohim), Greek: φοβοῦ τὸν θεόν, Aramaic: דחל לאלהא
translationNotes.note: Closing imperative in 5:7.

stories.keyTakeaway: Guard your steps at the house of God: draw near to listen, let your words be few before Him, and pay your vows without delay or excuse; Qohelet then observes officials watching officials over the oppressed, that he who loves money is never satisfied by money, that a man departs as naked as he came, and that to eat, drink, and find satisfaction in one’s labor is the gift of God.

stories.title: 💰 Ecclesiastes 6
summaryBullets: There is another evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily upon mankind: (6:1).

God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires; but God does not allow him to enjoy them. Instead, a stranger will enjoy them. This is futile and a grievous affliction. (6:2).

A man may father a hundred children and live for many years; yet no matter how long he lives, if he is unsatisfied with his prosperity and does not even receive a proper burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. (6:3).
For a stillborn child enters in futility and departs in darkness, and his name is shrouded in obscurity. (6:4).
The child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than that man, (6:5).
even if he lives a thousand years twice over but fails to enjoy his prosperity. Do not all go to the same place? (6:6).
All a man’s labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied. (6:7).
What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool? What gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others? (6:8).
Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind. (6:9).
Whatever exists was named long ago, and it is known what man is; but he cannot contend with one stronger than he. (6:10).
For the more words, the more futility — and how does that profit anyone? (6:11).
For who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow? Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun? (6:12).
crossRefs: Job 1:21: “Naked I came… naked shall I return” (cf. 5:15).
Proverbs 23:4-5: Riches sprout wings and fly away.
Psalm 39:6: People heap up wealth and do not know who will gather.
1 Timothy 6:6-10: On desire for riches and contentment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹשֶׁק / גֶּזֶל מִשְׁפָּט (ʿosheq / gezel mishpat); Greek (LXX): καταδυναστεία / ἀφαίρεσις κρίσεως
translationNotes.note: Named as observable in a province (5:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִתְרוֹן הָאָרֶץ (yitron ha’aretz); Greek: περισσεία τῆς γῆς
translationNotes.note: Difficult verse; states benefit/advantage tied to the field/land (5:9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּעִנְיַן רָע (beʿinyan raʿ); Greek (LXX): ἐν πραγματεία κακή
translationNotes.note: Phrase for a harmful business situation causing loss (5:14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֵפֶל (nefel), Greek (LXX): ἔκτρωμα, Aramaic: נפלא
translationNotes.note: Used for the comparison in 6:3-5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh), Greek (LXX): ψυχή, Aramaic: נפש
translationNotes.note: In 6:7-9 the “appetite/soul” not being filled is stated.

stories.keyTakeaway: Qohelet calls it a grievous evil that God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor yet a stranger enjoys them; a man who fathers a hundred children but cannot enjoy his prosperity is worse off than a stillborn child, for all go to the same place, the appetite is never satisfied, man cannot contend with one stronger than he, and no one knows what is good for him in his fleeting days.

stories.title: 🧭 Ecclesiastes 7
summaryBullets: A good name is better than fine perfume, and one’s day of death is better than his day of birth. (7:1).
It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart. (7:2).
Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart. (7:3).
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure. (7:4).
It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools. (7:5).
For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This too is futile. (7:6).
Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart. (7:7).
The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one. (7:8).
Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool. (7:9).
Do not say, “Why were the old days better than these?” For it is unwise of you to ask about this. (7:10).
Wisdom, like an inheritance, is good, and it benefits those who see the sun. (7:11).
For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner. (7:12).
Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent? (7:13).

In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him. (7:14).
In my futile life I have seen both of these: A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness. (7:15).
Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? (7:16).
Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time? (7:17).
It is good to grasp the one and not let the other slip from your hand. For he who fears God will follow both warnings. (7:18).
Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city. (7:19).
Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins. (7:20).
Do not pay attention to every word that is spoken, or you may hear your servant cursing you. (7:21).
For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others. (7:22).
All this I tested by wisdom, saying, “I resolve to be wise.” But it was beyond me. (7:23).
What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it? (7:24).
I directed my mind to understand, to explore, to search out wisdom and explanations, and to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness. (7:25).
And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are chains. The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared. (7:26).
“Behold,” says the Teacher, “I have discovered this by adding one thing to another to find an explanation. (7:27).
While my soul was still searching but not finding, among a thousand I have found one upright man, but among all these I have not found one such woman. (7:28).
Only this have I found: I have discovered that God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes.” (7:29).
crossRefs: Ecclesiastes 1:15: What is crooked cannot be made straight.
Job 2:10: “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?”
Proverbs 13:1: A wise son hears his father’s instruction (rebuke theme).
Proverbs 14:29: Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֵׁם (shem, ‘name’) / שֶׁמֶן (shemen, ‘oil’), Greek (LXX): ὄνομα / ἔλαιον, Aramaic: שמא / משחא
translationNotes.note: Sound-play in 7:1 highlighting valuing reputation over luxury.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית־אֵבֶל (beit-ʾevel), Greek: οἶκος πένθους, Aramaic: בית אבלא
translationNotes.note: Place of grieving; contrasted with house of feasting (7:2).

translationNotes.term: Crackling of thorns under a pot
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קוֹל הַסִּירִים תַּחַת הַסִּיר (qol ha-sirīm taḥat ha-sir); Greek: φωνὴ τῶν ἀκανθῶν ὑποκάτω τοῦ λέβητος
translationNotes.note: Quick, noisy burn of thorn-bushes; image for shallow laughter (7:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְתַקֵּן / עִוֵּת (letakken / ʿivvet), Greek: κατορθῶσαι / διεστραμμένον, Aramaic: תקן / עוות
translationNotes.note: Statement about the unalterable nature of God’s work (7:13).

stories.keyTakeaway: Better-than sayings prize a good name, the house of mourning, a wise man’s rebuke, patience, and the end of a matter; Qohelet adds that no one can straighten what God has bent, that God makes the day of prosperity and the day of adversity alike, that no righteous man on earth does good and never sins, that the woman who is a snare is more bitter than death, and that God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

stories.title: 👑 Ecclesiastes 8
summaryBullets: Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A man’s wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed. (8:1).
Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God. (8:2).
Do not hasten to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he will do whatever he pleases. (8:3).
For the king’s word is supreme, and who can say to him, “What are you doing?” (8:4).
Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm, and a wise heart knows the right time and procedure. (8:5).
For there is a right time and procedure to every purpose, though a man’s misery weighs heavily upon him. (8:6).
Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come? (8:7).
As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death. As no one can be discharged in wartime, so wickedness will not release those who practice it. (8:8).
All this I have seen, applying my mind to every deed that is done under the sun; there is a time when one man lords it over another to his own detriment. (8:9).
Then too, I saw the burial of the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place, and they were praised in the city where they had done so. This too is futile. (8:10).
When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil. (8:11).
Although a sinner does evil a hundred times and still lives long, yet I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence. (8:12).
Yet because the wicked do not fear God, it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow. (8:13).

There is a futility that is done on the earth: There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. I say that this too is futile. (8:14).

So I commended the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. For this joy will accompany him in his labor during the days of his life that God gives him under the sun. (8:15).
When I applied my mind to know wisdom and to observe the task that one performs on the earth — though his eyes do not see sleep in the day or even in the night — (8:16).

I saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning; even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend. (8:17).
crossRefs: Proverbs 24:21: Fear the LORD and the king.
Ecclesiastes 3:1; Ecclesiastes 3:17: A time and judgment for every matter.
Job 14:5: Man’s days are determined; limits on life.
Daniel 2:37: Royal authority described as given (power context).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁמוֹר פִּי־מֶלֶךְ (shemor pî-melech, ‘keep the mouth/command of the king’), Greek: φύλασσε τὸ ῥῆμα βασιλέως, Aramaic: נטר פוּם מלכא
translationNotes.note: “Mouth” idiom for royal decree (8:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁבֻעַת אֱלֹהִים (shevuʿat Elohim), Greek: ὅρκος θεοῦ, Aramaic: שבועתא דאלהא
translationNotes.note: Ground for obedience stated in 8:2.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ (ruaḥ), Greek: πνεῦμα, Aramaic: רוחא
translationNotes.note: Word can mean ‘wind’ or ‘spirit’; 8:8 states lack of control over it and over death.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְאֵין מִשְׁלַחַת בַּמִּלְחָמָה (veʾein mishlaḥat ba-milḥamah); Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπαλλαγὴ ἐν πολέμῳ
translationNotes.note: Expression that there is no exemption; the conflict binds those engaged (8:8).

stories.keyTakeaway: Keep the king’s command, for his word is supreme and no one has power over the wind or authority over the day of death; because sentence for a crime is not executed speedily, hearts fill with evil, yet it will go well with those who fear God, and though the righteous sometimes receive what the wicked deserve, Qohelet commends eating, drinking, and joy, for man cannot comprehend the work that is done under the sun.

stories.title: ⏳ Ecclesiastes 9
summaryBullets: So I took all this to heart and concluded that the righteous and the wise, as well as their deeds, are in God’s hands. Man does not know what lies ahead, whether love or hate. (9:1).

It is the same for all: There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked, for the good and the bad, for the clean and the unclean, for the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. As it is for the good, so it is for the sinner; as it is for the one who makes a vow, so it is for the one who refuses to take a vow. (9:2).

This is an evil in everything that is done under the sun: There is one fate for everyone. Furthermore, the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they are alive, and afterward they join the dead. (9:3).
There is hope, however, for anyone who is among the living; for even a live dog is better than a dead lion. (9:4).
For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. They have no further reward, because the memory of them is forgotten. (9:5).
Their love, their hate, and their envy have already vanished, and they will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun. (9:6).
Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved your works: (9:7).
Let your garments always be white, and never spare the oil for your head. (9:8).

Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun — all your fleeting days. For this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun. (9:9).
Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might, for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom. (9:10).

I saw something else under the sun: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent, nor the favor to the skillful. For time and chance happen to all. (9:11).
For surely no man knows his time: Like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare, so men are ensnared in an evil time that suddenly falls upon them. (9:12).
I have also seen this wisdom under the sun, and it was great to me: (9:13).
There was a small city with few men. A mighty king came against it, surrounded it, and built large siege ramps against it. (9:14).
Now a poor wise man was found in the city, and he saved the city by his wisdom. Yet no one remembered that poor man. (9:15).
And I said, “Wisdom is better than strength, but the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.” (9:16).
The calm words of the wise are heeded over the shouts of a ruler among fools. (9:17).
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good. (9:18).
crossRefs: Ecclesiastes 12:7: The same book ends with the dust returning to the ground it came from and the spirit returning to God who gave it.
Ecclesiastes 12:13-14: The book's closing sentence puts everything under judgment: God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.
Daniel 12:2: 'Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.'
Psalms 49:10-12: Wise men die, and so do the fool and the stupid, and they leave their wealth to others, which is the same observation 9:2-3 makes.
Genesis 3:19: 'For dust you are, and to dust you shall return', the sentence the whole book measures a lifetime against.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּגָדִים לְבָנִים / שֶׁמֶן (begadim levanim / shemen); Greek: ἱμάτια λευκά / ἔλαιον
translationNotes.note: Festive/joy imagery in 9:8.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵת וָפֶגַע (ʿet va-pegaʿ); Greek (LXX): καιρὸς καὶ συνάντημα
translationNotes.note: Stated as happening to all (9:11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵלֶק (ḥeleq), Greek: μερὶς, Aramaic: חולקה
translationNotes.note: Share/lot; repeated theme for daily enjoyment (9:9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)
translationNotes.note: The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ (tachat hashemesh)
translationNotes.note: This is the book's own statement of where it is standing, and it occurs twenty-nine times, from the opening question at 1:3 onward. It marks what can be observed from inside this life and this world. It is attached directly to the statement about the dead here: 9:6 says they will never again have a share in anything that is done under the sun. The same book then speaks from outside that vantage at 12:7, where the spirit returns to God who gave it, and at 12:14, where God brings every deed into judgment.

stories.keyTakeaway: The righteous and the wise and their deeds are in God’s hands, and one fate comes to all, so Qohelet urges eating bread with joy, enjoying life with your beloved wife, and working with all your might, for in Sheol there is no work or knowledge. The race is not to the swift, for time and chance happen to all; a poor wise man saves a small besieged city by his wisdom yet is forgotten, and wisdom is better than strength, better than weapons of war, though one sinner destroys much good.

headings.text: Death Comes to Good and Bad
Enjoy Your Portion in This Life

stories.title: 🧩 Ecclesiastes 10
summaryBullets: As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor. (10:1).
A wise man’s heart inclines to the right, but the heart of a fool to the left. (10:2).
Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool. (10:3).
If the ruler’s temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest. (10:4).
There is an evil I have seen under the sun — an error that proceeds from the ruler: (10:5).
Folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions. (10:6).
I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves. (10:7).
He who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake. (10:8).
The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself. (10:9).
If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success. (10:10).
If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer. (10:11).
The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him. (10:12).
The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness. (10:13).
Yet the fool multiplies words. No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him? (10:14).
The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city. (10:15).
Woe to you, O land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning. (10:16).
Blessed are you, O land whose king is a son of nobles, and whose princes feast at the proper time— for strength and not for drunkenness. (10:17).
Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks. (10:18).
A feast is prepared for laughter, and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything. (10:19).
Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech. (10:20).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 20:16-22: A wise woman delivers a city under siege (parallel deliverance theme).
Proverbs 26:27: He who digs a pit will fall into it.
Proverbs 10:19: When words are many, transgression is not lacking.
Psalm 75:6-7: Promotion comes not from the east or west but God exalts and brings low (rulers theme).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְבוּבֵי מָוֶת (zevuvê mavet, ‘flies of death’) / רוֹקֵחַ (roqe’aḥ, ‘perfumer’); Greek (LXX): μύρα
translationNotes.note: Image for small folly ruining valued substance (10:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְמִין / שְׂמֹאל (yemin / semol); Greek: δεξιὰ / ἀριστερά
translationNotes.note: Directional contrast used for wise/foolish disposition (10:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּי עוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם יוֹלִיךְ אֶת־הַקּוֹל (ki ʿof ha-shamayim yolikh et ha-qol); Greek (LXX): ὅτι πετεινὸν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀξει τὴν φωνήν
translationNotes.note: Figure for secret speech being reported (10:20).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לַחַשׁ (laḥash, ‘incantation’) / לֹחֵשׁ (loḥesh, ‘charmer’); Greek (LXX): ἐπῳδή / ἐπῳδός
translationNotes.note: 10:11 image: a snake that bites before a charm is uttered yields no advantage.

stories.keyTakeaway: As dead flies foul the perfumer’s oil, a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor; sayings contrast the wise and the fool in speech and work, note folly appointed to great heights while princes go on foot like slaves, pronounce woe on a land whose king is a youth, and warn against cursing the king even in thought, for a bird of the air may carry the word.

stories.title: 🌱 Ecclesiastes 11
summaryBullets: Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again. (11:1).
Divide your portion among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what disaster may befall the land. (11:2).
If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain upon the earth; whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where it falls, there it will lie. (11:3).
He who watches the wind will fail to sow, and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap. (11:4).
As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things. (11:5).
Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper. (11:6).
Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun. (11:7).
So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all. But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. Everything to come is futile. (11:8).

Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment. (11:9).
So banish sorrow from your heart, and cast off pain from your body, for youth and vigor are fleeting. (11:10).
crossRefs: Genesis 8:22: Seedtime and harvest shall not cease.
Proverbs 11:24-25: On giving and generosity.
John 3:8: The wind/spirit blows where it wishes (language parallel).
Ecclesiastes 3:11: Humans cannot find out the work God has done from beginning to end.

translationNotes.term: Cast your bread upon the waters
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁלַּח לַחְמְךָ עַל־פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם (shallakh laḥmekha ʿal penei ha-mayim), Greek (LXX): ἀπόστειλον τὸν ἄρτον σου ἐπὶ πρόσωπον τοῦ ὕδατος, Aramaic: שלח לחמך על אפי מיא
translationNotes.note: Figurative instruction in 11:1 stated as written, without specifying a particular commercial or charitable interpretation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׁבְעָה… וְגַם לִשְׁמוֹנָה (shivʿah… ve-gam li-shmonah); Greek: ἑπτά… καὶ ὀκτώ
translationNotes.note: Numerical intensification formula (laddered numbers) in 11:2.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ (ruaḥ), Greek: πνεῦμα, Aramaic: רוחא
translationNotes.note: Word can mean wind or spirit; 11:5 states human ignorance of its way.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּעֲצָמִים בְּבֶטֶן הַמְלֵאָה (kaʿatsamim be-veten ha-mele’ah); Greek (LXX): ὡς τὰ ὀστέα ἐν κοιλίᾳ τῆς κυοφορούσης
translationNotes.note: Growth in utero cited as an example of unknown process (11:5).

stories.keyTakeaway: Cast your bread upon the waters and divide your portion among seven or eight; sow in the morning and do not rest in the evening, for no one knows which will succeed, just as no one knows the path of the wind or the work of God who makes all things. Light is sweet, so let a man rejoice in all his years while remembering that the days of darkness will be many, and let the young man rejoice in his youth, knowing that for all these things God will bring him to judgment.

headings.text: Cast Your Bread upon the Waters

stories.title: 🌅 Ecclesiastes 12
summaryBullets: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come and the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,” (12:1).
before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain, (12:2).
on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop, when those grinding cease because they are few and those watching through windows see dimly, (12:3).
when the doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades away, when one rises at the sound of a bird and all the daughters of song grow faint, (12:4).

when men fear the heights and dangers of the road, when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring, and the caper berry shrivels — for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets. (12:5).
Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed, before the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well, (12:6).
before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it. (12:7).
“Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher. “Everything is futile!” (12:8).
Not only was the Teacher wise, but he also taught the people knowledge; he pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs. (12:9).
The Teacher searched to find delightful sayings and to record accurate words of truth. (12:10).
The words of the wise are like goads, and the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd. (12:11).
And by these, my son, be further warned: There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body. (12:12).
When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man. (12:13).
For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil. (12:14).
crossRefs: Genesis 3:19: Dust to dust (cf. Ecclesiastes 12:7).
Psalm 90:10: The span and weariness of human life.
Ecclesiastes 3:20: All go to one place; all are from dust and to dust return.
Jeremiah 9:17-18: Mourning women and public lament (mourner imagery).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְכֹר אֶת־בּוֹרְאֶיךָ (zekhor et-bor’eikha), Greek (LXX): μνήσθητι τοῦ κτίστου σου, Aramaic: דכור לבראך
translationNotes.note: Imperative in 12:1 placed before the imagery of decline.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַנֵּאץ הַשָּׁקֵד (ha-shaqed yane’etz); Greek (LXX): ἀνθήσει τὸ ἀμύγδαλον
translationNotes.note: Seasonal blooming image in 12:5.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְיִסְתַּפֵּל הָאֲבִיּוֹנָה (ve-yistappēl ha-ʾaviyyōnāh); Greek (LXX): καὶ διασκεδασθήσεται ἡ κάππαρις
translationNotes.note: Rare word 12:5 (caperberry); stated as failing/ineffective.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ (beit ʿolamo); Greek (LXX): οἶκον αἰῶνος
translationNotes.note: Destination phrase in 12:5.

translationNotes.term: Silver cord / golden bowl / pitcher / wheel
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֶּסֶר הַכֶּסֶף / גֻלַּת הַזָּהָב / כַּד / גַּלְגַּל; Greek (LXX): σπεῖραμα ἀργύρινον / φιάλη χρυσῆ / κάδος / τροχός
translationNotes.note: Sequence of breaking/shattering images in 12:6.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְהָרוּחַ תָּשׁוּב אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים (ve-ha-ruaḥ tashuv el-ha’Elohim); Greek (LXX): καὶ ἐπιστρέψει τὸ πνεῦμα πρὸς τὸν θεόν
translationNotes.note: Statement in 12:7 parallel to dust returning to earth.

stories.keyTakeaway: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the keepers of the house tremble, the silver cord is snapped, the dust returns to the ground, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. The Teacher repeats that everything is futile, then, as one who taught the people knowledge and arranged many proverbs, gives the conclusion of the matter: fear God and keep His commandments, for God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing.

intro:
Ecclesiastes was written by Solomon, son of David and third king of Israel, who identifies himself in the opening line as "the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem" (1:1, 1:12). Jewish tradition holds that Solomon composed the book in his old age, late in his reign around 935 BC, after authoring Song of Songs in his youth and Proverbs in his middle years. The same Solomon who wrote Proverbs and Song of Songs; Ecclesiastes belongs to his old-age reflections on a long life. He reigned over a united Israel from Jerusalem for forty years (c. 970-931 BC), the son of David and Bathsheba; God appeared to him at Gibeon at the start of his reign and granted him unmatched wisdom along with riches and honor (1 Kings 3:5-14). He built the first temple in seven years, expanded the kingdom's territory and trade networks to their greatest historical extent, married seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines from foreign nations, and turned in his later years to the worship of the foreign gods of his wives (1 Kings 11:1-8). The historical setting is the closing decades of the United Monarchy, with Israel at its territorial and economic peak, trading with Tyre under Hiram I (Phoenicia), Sheba (modern Yemen), and Egypt's 21st Dynasty; Israel's neighbors (Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Aramaean states) remained subjugated; and the Neo-Assyrian Empire was rising in the north but had not yet pressed into the Levant.

Ecclesiastes is the twenty-first book of the Christian Old Testament. In the Hebrew Bible it is one of the Five Megillot (Five Scrolls) within the Ketuvim (Writings), traditionally read aloud in synagogues at the Feast of Sukkot (Tabernacles, the autumn harvest festival). The Hebrew name Qoheleth (קֹהֶלֶת) is a participle derived from the root qahal ("to assemble") and refers to one who gathers or addresses an assembly, hence "the Teacher," "the Preacher," or "the Assembler"; the title functions as the author's self-designation throughout the book. The English title "Ecclesiastes" comes from the Greek Septuagint Ekklesiastes (3rd century BC, from ekklesia, "assembly"), the Greek rendering of Qoheleth. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Ecclesiastes were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with two scrolls (4QQoha and 4QQohb) dating to the 2nd century BC.
